title: Shared Responsibility Model
summary: Where the cloud provider's security obligation ends and the customer's begins, and how that line moves across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

slides.markdown:
Moving to the cloud does not mean the cloud provider is now responsible for your security. It means the responsibility is **split**, and exactly where the split falls is the single most misunderstood fact in cloud security — and one of the most expensive to get wrong.

The **shared responsibility model** draws that line explicitly: the provider secures the infrastructure underneath the service, and the customer secures what they build and configure on top of it. Almost every major cloud breach in the last decade that made headlines — an exposed S3 bucket, a misconfigured database with no auth — was a failure on the customer's side of that line, not a provider vulnerability.

slides.sectionTitle: Security "of" the cloud vs "in" the cloud
slides.markdown:
AWS's own phrasing draws the cleanest version of the line, and it generalizes to every provider:

- **Security *of* the cloud** — the provider's job. Physical data center security, the hypervisor, the underlying network hardware, and the managed service's own code (e.g., the database engine's internals for a managed database).
- **Security *in* the cloud** — the customer's job. How you configure the services you use: IAM policies, network rules, what data goes where, whether encryption is turned on, how your application code handles secrets.

The provider is responsible for the platform being trustworthy; you're responsible for using it correctly. A provider can have a flawless security record on their half of the line and you can still get breached entirely through your half — an open S3 bucket isn't AWS's failure, it's a bucket policy someone left wide open.

slides.sectionTitle: How the line shifts across IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
slides.markdown:
| | IaaS (e.g. a raw VM) | PaaS (e.g. a managed database or app platform) | SaaS (e.g. a hosted email or CRM product) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Provider secures | Physical hardware, hypervisor, network | + the OS, runtime, and platform software | + the application itself |
| Customer secures | OS patching, network config, application, data, IAM | Application code, data, access configuration, IAM | Access configuration, data, user permissions |
| Customer's OS-level work | Full — you patch and harden the OS yourself | None — provider patches the underlying OS | None — no OS exposure at all |

The further up this stack you go, the more the provider absorbs — but the customer's slice never reaches zero. Even on a fully-managed SaaS product, you still own who has access, what permissions they hold, and what data you put into it. "We use SaaS, so security is the vendor's problem" is the same category of mistake as assuming a locked building means you don't need a lock on your own office door inside it.

slides.subTitle: Mistakenly blamed on "the cloud"
slides.markdown:
A pattern that repeats across nearly every major cloud data exposure: the underlying platform worked exactly as designed, and the failure was a customer-side configuration choice.

- **Publicly readable storage buckets** — a storage bucket (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) left with public or overly broad read access, usually by accident or by a default that was never revisited.
- **Databases with no authentication required**, exposed directly to the internet because a network rule was too permissive.
- **Overly broad IAM roles** — a role that grants far more access than the workload needs, so a single compromised service credential reaches far more than it should.
- **Unencrypted data at rest** left on the customer, in providers where encryption is opt-in rather than default.

None of these are provider vulnerabilities. The provider gave you the tool (a bucket, a database, an IAM system) and the controls to configure it correctly — the security failure is in how those controls were used, which is precisely the customer's half of the line.

slides.sectionTitle: An IaaS VM breach vs a SaaS misconfiguration
slides.subTitle: Whose failure is it?
slides.markdown:
| Scenario | Whose responsibility was violated? |
|---|---|
| An attacker exploits an unpatched OS vulnerability on a customer-managed VM | Customer — OS patching is explicitly the customer's job on IaaS |
| An attacker exploits a vulnerability in the hypervisor itself, escaping to another customer's VM | Provider — the hypervisor is squarely "security of the cloud" |
| An employee at a company grants a SaaS CRM's built-in "export all records" permission to every user by mistake | Customer — access configuration is the customer's job even on SaaS |
| The SaaS vendor's own application has an authentication bypass bug | Provider — the application's own code is their responsibility on SaaS |

The pattern: ask *which layer* the failure occurred in, then ask who owns that layer for the specific service model in use. The same category of mistake (a permission misconfiguration) can be squarely the customer's fault on SaaS while a comparable-sounding OS-level compromise is squarely the customer's fault on IaaS too — it's the layer that decides, not which side sounds more sympathetic.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the model matters for incident response and audits
slides.markdown:
Beyond a conceptual line, the shared responsibility model shapes two very practical things. In an **incident**, it determines who's actually able to investigate what: a customer generally can't get low-level hypervisor logs from their provider (that's the provider's operational domain), but the provider can't see inside your application's business logic or your IAM policy history — you own producing that evidence.

In a **compliance audit** (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, HIPAA), the provider typically supplies their own third-party audit report covering their half of the line (a SOC 2 report, for instance), and the customer is still separately responsible for proving they configured their half correctly — using the provider's compliant infrastructure does not automatically make your application compliant. Auditors ask for both: the provider's attestation and your own configuration evidence.

A team that hasn't internalized the model tends to get this backwards during an actual incident — wasting time asking the provider for something only the customer can produce, or assuming the provider's compliance certification covers gaps that are explicitly on the customer's side of the line.

slides.sectionTitle: Managed services still leave a customer slice
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
The subtle trap for experienced engineers: as services get more managed, the *shape* of the customer's remaining responsibility changes, but its *importance* doesn't shrink proportionally. On a managed database (PaaS), you no longer patch the database engine — but you still choose the network access rules, the IAM policy for who can query it, whether encryption at rest uses a provider-managed or customer-managed key, and how backups are protected. Get any of those wrong and the database engine being perfectly patched by the provider doesn't help you at all.

In fact, the *smaller and more concentrated* customer-side surface on a heavily managed service often makes the remaining choices matter more, not less — there are fewer knobs, but each one now carries more of the total risk. A single overly permissive IAM policy on a fully-managed service can be the entire security posture failing at once, precisely because everything else was already handled well by the provider.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming the provider secures your data by default
slides.markdown:
The pitfall to name directly: assuming that because a big, reputable cloud provider hosts your data, the data itself is automatically secured. It isn't — the provider secures the platform; whether encryption is enabled, whether access is scoped correctly, and whether that storage bucket is actually private are configuration choices that live squarely on the customer's side of the line, and many of them default to permissive rather than restrictive unless explicitly changed.

This mistake shows up constantly in headline breaches: "AWS was hacked" is almost never the accurate description of what happened; "a customer left an S3 bucket publicly readable" usually is. The provider's infrastructure worked exactly as designed in nearly every one of these incidents.

The fix is treating every managed service's default configuration as something to actively verify, not trust — check whether encryption is on, whether network access is scoped to what's needed, and whether IAM grants are least-privilege, rather than assuming the provider's reputation implies your specific configuration is safe.
